source: Over the past decade, there has been a steady rise in the proportion of emotionally negative songs topping the Billboard charts, reflecting a broader shift in popular music's emotional landscape.
why: The year-by-year share does not rise steadily: it falls from 30.2% in 2015 to 27.3% in 2016 and from 55.6% in 2018 to 37.8% in 2019 before reaching 49.2% in 2020. The broader upward trend is captured in the negative-song-trend-up fact using the story's other wording ('clear upward trend ... particularly since the mid-2010s').

source: In 2020, for the first time in the history of our dataset, negative songs outnumbered positive ones in the year-end top 10.
why: The file has 31 negative and 32 positive top-10 songs in 2020 (49.2% negative, 50.8% positive). The only year from 1960-2020 with a negative majority is 2018 (35 negative, 28 positive, 55.6%), so 2020 is neither a negative majority nor the first. The file contains no Billboard year-end-chart rank with which to apply a 'year-end top 10' definition.

source: Interestingly, this shift coincides with the rise of Hip hop/Rap as the dominant genre in popular music, overtaking the more traditionally upbeat Pop.
why: billboard.csv has no genre column, so the claimed genre ranking and its coincidence with the sentiment trend cannot be computed.

source: Hip hop songs, on average, tend to have a much higher proportion of negative emotions compared to other genres.
why: billboard.csv has no genre column, so songs cannot be grouped into Hip hop versus other genres.

source: But this is not to say that negativity is confined to Hip hop. Across the board, from Pop to Rock to R&B, songs with darker themes have been on the ascent.
why: billboard.csv has no genre column, so the cross-genre claim cannot be checked.

source: Some, like Billie Eilish or Juice WRLD, are known for their consistently dark and moody lyrics, while others, like Ariana Grande or BTS, tend towards a more positive, uplifting tone.
why: Using the performer field as the story does (multi-artist strings are not split among the named artists), the 1960-2020 shares of songs classified as negative are: Juice WRLD 100% (3 songs), Billie Eilish 50% (4), Ariana Grande 44.4% (9) and BTS 25% (4). Billie Eilish and Ariana Grande are nearly identical, so the stated pairing of Eilish/Juice WRLD as dark against Ariana Grande/BTS as positive is not reproduced; the text also gives no numeric artist scores to check against the 'Artist Sentiment Scores' chart.

source: What's fascinating is how an artist's emotional fingerprint can evolve over their career, often reflecting their personal growth and struggles.
why: This is a general qualitative claim with no named artist, period, or number to compute; the specific Taylor Swift case is covered by the taylor-swift-darker fact.
